title: To Live Is Christ, to Die Is Gain
summary: Paul greets the church at Philippi, thanks God with joy for their partnership in the gospel, and prays that their love will grow in knowledge and discernment. He reports that his imprisonment has actually advanced the gospel, since the palace guard knows why he is in chains and other believers have grown bolder, and he rejoices that Christ is preached even by rivals. Facing possible death, he weighs departing to be with Christ against remaining for their sake, expects to remain, and urges the church to live as citizens worthy of the gospel, standing firm together without fear.
story: Paul had founded the church at Philippi about a decade earlier, on his second missionary trip (Acts 16), and it had stood by him ever since. Now he is in prison, and the Philippians have sent Epaphroditus with a gift. This first chapter answers their concern about him. Instead of dwelling on his own hardship he tells them how the gospel is advancing, and he turns his possible death into a reflection on what life is for. The chapter introduces the themes that run through the whole letter: joy in hard circumstances, partnership in the gospel, the day of Christ, and the call to unity. Its closing appeal to stand firm in one spirit (v. 27) leads directly into chapter 2's call to share the mind of Christ.
historical:
Paul writes in chains (vv. 7, 13, 14, 17). Where he was held is debated: Rome, where he was under house arrest around AD 60 to 62 (Acts 28:16, 30), is the traditional view; Ephesus in the mid-50s and Caesarea in the late 50s are the main alternatives (see the introduction). The palace guard (v. 13) translates the Latin loanword praetorium, which could mean the emperor's Praetorian Guard in Rome or the headquarters of a provincial governor, such as Herod's praetorium in Caesarea (Acts 23:35). The word fits each view.

Paul's case was apparently still undecided, and the outcome could be execution (vv. 20-23). The rivals who preached Christ out of envy (vv. 15-17) were evidently Christians in the city of his imprisonment who saw his chains as an opportunity to advance themselves. Paul does not accuse them of false teaching, only of bad motives, which is why he can rejoice in their preaching. The church in Philippi was facing opponents of its own (v. 28), probably local pressure on believers who would not honor the gods and the emperor as their neighbors did.
cultural:
The letter begins with overseers and deacons (v. 1), one of the earliest references to recognized leaders in a local church. Overseer (episkopos) later became the word for bishop, but here the title is plural and describes a group of leaders, probably the same people elsewhere called elders; deacon (diakonos) means servant or minister. How these offices developed is discussed in the Pastoral Letters.

Philippi was a Roman colony whose people were proud of their citizenship. In verse 27, where the BSB has conduct yourselves, Paul uses a verb that means to live as a citizen or to carry out one's civic duties. He is telling people who knew what it meant to represent Rome far from Rome that they now represent another kingdom. His talk of chains would also have carried weight in an honor-conscious culture, where imprisonment brought shame on the prisoner and his friends; Paul reframes his chains as a badge of service to Christ, and the Philippians' support as a share in that honor.
literary: The chapter follows the shape of an ancient letter, filled with Christian content: greeting (vv. 1-2), thanksgiving and prayer (vv. 3-11), a report on the writer's circumstances (vv. 12-26), and the first appeal (vv. 27-30). The thanksgiving is warm and personal, full of words for all of you, joy, and affection. Paul's report turns on repeated rejoicing (v. 18) and on the tension between two good outcomes. Verse 19 echoes the words of Job in the Greek Old Testament (Job 13:16), where Job trusts that his situation will turn out for his deliverance; Paul, like Job, expects vindication before God whatever human judges decide. Verse 21 compresses his outlook into two short, balanced clauses: “For to me, to live is Christ, and to die is gain.”

outline.t: Thanksgiving for partnership in the gospel
Prayer for love, discernment, and fruit
Chains that advance the gospel; Christ is preached
To live is Christ, to die is gain
Live worthy of the gospel and stand firm together

doctrines.note: Paul sees God at work in his imprisonment: what looked like a setback has served to advance the gospel (v. 12). God's purpose is not stopped by chains, rivals, or the threat of death.

God began a good work in the believers and will carry it on to completion until the day of Christ (v. 6). Salvation is God's work from start to finish, and Paul's confidence rests on God's faithfulness rather than theirs.

Suffering for Christ is described as something granted, a gift, alongside believing in him (v. 29). It is not a sign that God has abandoned his people but a share in the same struggle Paul and Christ himself faced.
For Paul, death is gain because it means to depart and be with Christ, which is far better (v. 23). Christian hope looks beyond death to being with Christ, while still valuing life as fruitful labor.

words.note: Koinonia, partnership, fellowship, participation, or sharing. It means having something in common, and in verse 5 it describes the Philippians' active share in Paul's work: their prayer, their money, and their sending of Epaphroditus. Fellowship in the New Testament is not only friendship but joint commitment to a common cause.

Praitorion, praetorium, a Latin word borrowed into Greek. It could mean the headquarters of a Roman governor, the governor's residence, or the Praetorian Guard, the emperor's elite troops in Rome. Its meaning in verse 13 is tied to the debate over where Paul was imprisoned.

Politeuomai, to live as a citizen, to conduct one's public life. Paul uses it in verse 27 instead of his usual verb for walking. In a Roman colony the word would have been heard in political terms: believers are to carry out their civic life as citizens of Christ's kingdom (compare 3:20).

Kerdos, gain or profit, a commercial word. To die is gain (v. 21) because death brings Paul into Christ's presence. The word returns in 3:7, where Paul says whatever was gain to him he now counts as loss for Christ.

christ: Christ is the center of Paul's life in this chapter, not just of his beliefs. He loves the Philippians with the affection of Christ Jesus (v. 8). His chains are for Christ (v. 13). His joy is that Christ is preached (v. 18). His hope is that Christ will be exalted in his body, whether by life or by death (v. 20). His very definition of life is Christ (v. 21), and the best thing he can imagine after death is to be with Christ (v. 23). The day of Christ (vv. 6, 10), his return, is the horizon toward which the church's life moves. And believers suffer on behalf of Christ (v. 29), which ties their lives to the pattern of his own, a pattern chapter 2 will describe in full.

hard.q: What happens when a believer dies? Does Paul mean he will be with Christ at once?
hard.a:
Paul says that to depart is to be with Christ, which is far better (v. 23), and most Christians through history have read this as teaching that believers who die go at once into Christ's presence, even before the resurrection of the body at his return. This is often called the intermediate state: a real but incomplete existence with Christ between death and resurrection. It fits other texts such as 2 Corinthians 5:8, where to be away from the body is to be at home with the Lord, and Jesus's words to the thief on the cross (Luke 23:43).

A minority of Christians, sometimes called Christian mortalists, hold that the dead are unconscious (soul sleep) until the resurrection, so that departing and being with Christ are experienced as immediate even though time passes. They point to the New Testament's frequent description of death as sleep. Both views affirm what Paul teaches elsewhere with great emphasis, that the final hope is not escape from the body but the resurrection of the body at Christ's return (3:20-21).

questions: Paul turned his imprisonment into an opportunity. What circumstance in your life might God be using in a way you haven't noticed?
Paul rejoiced that Christ was preached even by people with bad motives. What does that suggest about how to respond to rivals in ministry?
How would you finish Paul's sentence, “For to me, to live is …”? What would it take for your honest answer to be Christ?
